name: Rice water rinse

lead: Rice water is the starchy liquid from soaking, rinsing or boiling rice, often fermented for a day or two, then applied to hair after shampoo. People use it for stronger strands, less breakage, more shine and longer hair.

Believers credit inositol, amino acids and starch for coating or entering the strand, cutting friction and breakage, while fermentation adds acidity. Women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia have reportedly used it for centuries, but studies of rice water itself are limited, and small trials that exist mostly looked at rice bran products.

paras: People soak or boil rice, strain the liquid, sometimes ferment it for a day or two, and pour it over hair and scalp after shampooing for a few minutes before rinsing. It is used weekly or so as a treatment step. Users report changes in shine and softness quickly and in length only over months.

Protein or starch buildup can leave hair dry, stiff or brittle, especially curly hair. Rice can carry arsenic, which is mainly a concern for ingestion. Rice water that has spoiled is discarded rather than used.

angle.text: Rice water rinses are used for stronger, shinier hair that breaks less and looks longer. The reasoning is that starch and amino acids coat the strand and cut friction. It has centuries of traditional use, and research on rice water itself is limited.

lead: A rice water rinse is a hair treatment in which the starchy liquid left from soaking, rinsing or boiling rice, often fermented for a day or two, is applied to the hair and scalp after shampooing. People use it to get smoother, shinier, stronger-feeling hair that breaks less, and many hope it helps hair reach greater length [1][1].

Wikipedia states that women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia have reportedly used rice water on hair for centuries, and that women in Japan's Heian period (794-1185) were reportedly able to keep very long, healthy hair by washing it in rice water [2]. The best-known modern reference is the Yao women of Huangluo, China, whose long hair is attributed by themselves and by popular media to daily fermented rice rinses [1].

Proponents credit amino acids and inositol, a carbohydrate, for reduced friction, better elasticity and less breakage. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that strong scientific evidence for faster growth or added length is lacking and that claims are largely anecdotal [1][1]. The rinse appears in K-beauty hair routines and in hair-growth discussions on forums, where one T Nation thread describes people being 'all over' fermented rice water alongside minoxidil [3].
infobox: About 12 to 48 hours at room temperature [1]

paras: Rice water is a starchy, milky liquid obtained by soaking, rinsing or boiling rice; Grokipedia distinguishes plain rice water, fermented rice water left at room temperature for roughly 12 to 48 hours, and boiled rice water [1]. For hair, Grokipedia describes use as a rinse after shampooing, and as a base mixed into masks with oils [1]. Fermentation is said to acidify the liquid [1].

Wikipedia's article on rice water notes that women in parts of Asia, including China, Japan and Southeast Asia, have used it on hair for centuries, and links the practice to women of Japan's Heian period (794-1185 CE), who reportedly had very long hair that stayed healthy after washing in it [2]. The same article also records long use of rice water as a food, including for digestive problems [2].

Proponents attribute benefits to amino acids and inositol, a carbohydrate said to reduce friction, improve elasticity and limit breakage, possibly by penetrating the hair shaft; Grokipedia states that this has not been established for rice water specifically [1]. The cultural reference most cited is the Yao women of Huangluo, China, whose long hair is attributed by themselves and by popular media to daily fermented rice water rinses [1].

Grokipedia reports that protein or starch buildup may cause dryness, stiffness or brittleness, especially in curly or coily hair, and that low- and high-porosity hair may respond differently [1]. It also notes that rice can accumulate arsenic, which is a concern mainly for internal consumption [1].

No studies found of rice water rinses in people. Grokipedia says a 2022 systematic review reported possible benefits for hair strength and breakage over 8 to 12 weeks, but that it mainly covered rice bran extracts and related products rather than rice water, and that the trials had fewer than 50 participants each [1]. That summary is from an AI-generated source and is not a primary study.

Rice water is discussed as a low-cost home remedy next to products such as minoxidil. A T Nation forum user wrote that people were 'all over using fermented rice water' while placing minoxidil and Monistat shampoo as the products they consider known to work [3].

lore.intro: Rice water is discussed in beauty and hair-growth circles as a traditional remedy, frequently linked to the long hair of Yao women in Huangluo and to the K-beauty trend [1][3].

claims.claim: Fermented rice water makes hair grow longer.
Rice water strengthens hair and reduces breakage.
Rice water is a hair-growth rival to minoxidil.

timeline.event: Heian period in Japan, during which women are reported to have used rice water on their hair [2].
